text:
matt: Heads-up — we have a perf regression that looks tied to kernel selection + batching heuristics + KV cache churn. Need a safe plan to profile prod traces (nsys/nvprof/perfetto) without blowing latency or SLOs. Thoughts on sampling vs full tracing and concrete guardrails?

jessica: Short answer: sample first. Full timeline traces are super useful but heavy. Our usual stack: Nsight Systems (nsys) + NVTX annotations, export to perfetto for combined CPU/GPU timeline.

matt: Any rough overhead numbers to cite when convincing infra/security?

jessica: Ballpark: full, continuous nsys timeline with CUPTI callbacks & all kernels can add noticeable overhead — we’ve seen anywhere from ~20% up to 50–80% depending on workload and capture verbosity. Sampling or light traces usually in the ~2–8% range. Perfetto CPU-only collection is pretty cheap.

linh: Operational guardrails that work for us: 1) only run on canary/dedicated nodes (no traffic to customer critical hosts), 2) sample a tiny fraction of requests (e.g. 0.5–2%), 3) timebox each capture window (30–60s), 4) auto-stop if p95 latency or error rate ticks up beyond a small threshold.

jessica: Also: instrument NVTX ranges around key runtime regions (batching window open/close, kv cache lookup/hit/miss, kernel dispatch). That makes post-hoc hotspot identification way faster. Add lightweight counters for cache hits/misses in logs to correlate with traces.

matt: Can you drop an example nsys command we can use as a baseline?

jessica: Example (start here and tune flags):
```
nsys profile --output prod_canary_trace \
  --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --capture-range=nvtx \
  --sample=cpu --stop-on-exit \
  --time-limit 30s \
  -- python -u server.py
```
Notes: --sample reduces CUPTI overhead vs full callbacks. Use --capture-range=nvtx to only record when we push NVTX ranges around the request handling.

ryan: We shouldn't run the server under profiler in main prod fleet. Prefer creating a canary deployment and shadow a small % of traffic to it (or replay from recorded traces). Sidecar capture is also an option.

jessica: If you need even lower overhead for live sampling consider NCU/CUPTI sampling modes or host perf/event-based sampling for CPU hot paths. For kernel timelines perfetto + nsys export gives the combined view. nvprof is deprecated — don't use it for new captures.

matt: How do we detect KV-cache related regressions specifically? Evictions and memcpy spikes?

linh: Yeah — instrument right before cache lookup and after. In traces look for: cache-miss -> memcpy (host->device) -> long kernel launch(s). Also watch for sudden increase in Vram traffic and more frequent small kernels (eviction/restore churn). Correlate with the cache-size metric and eviction counters we emit.

jessica: For profiling windows include a reproducible warmup pattern: run warmup requests so KV cache reaches steady state, then start capture. That avoids chasing transient cold-miss noise.

profiling-bot: Reminder: when capturing in prod/canary set retention TTL for raw traces, scrub PII, and run under approved ticket. Upload traces to secure bucket and rotate access keys. :lock:

matt: Plan: spin a canary fleet, shadow ~1% of traffic, NVTX annotations + 30s sample windows, store raw traces to s3://redwood-traces/prod-canary with 14d TTL. If p95 > baseline+5% stop profiling automatically. @ryan can you provision temporary bucket & creds?

ryan: On it — will create bucket with temp creds and post vault path here when ready.

linh: I'll schedule the first capture tomorrow 08:30 PST and post a short kernel-timeline screenshot + notes.

matt: Awesome — thanks. After the first set we'll look for kernel selection anomalies (unexpected heavy kernels), batching windows that starve smaller requests, and any KV eviction bursts.

jessica: Quick checklist to include in the ticket: NVTX ranges for request/batch/cache; warmup-run before capture; sampling-mode nsys command; timebox and stop-on-slo-breach; secure upload + TTL; canary-only.

matt: Adding that to the ticket now.
